Each also has .y and .z, for work that is naturally a picture or a volume.

The two lines that start every kernel

int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
if (i < n) ...

The first line turns "thread 5 of block 2" into "element 517". The second is there because the launch rounds up to whole blocks: 1000 elements with 256 threads per block need 4 blocks, which is 1024 threads, and the last 24 have nothing to do. Without the check they write past the end of the array. A GPU gives no error for that. It corrupts whatever was there.

The number of blocks is n divided by the block size, rounded up:

int blocks = (n + threads_per_block - 1) / threads_per_block;

No order is promised

The threads run in whatever order the device likes, and many run at the same instant. Three rules follow, and the exercises are built around them:

  • Each thread writes only its own output. Then the order cannot matter.
  • To read neighbours, read from one array and write to another. Otherwise a thread may see a neighbour before or after its update.
  • Never add into one shared variable. That is the race from the lesson before, a thousand times over. Build sums in rounds, pair by pair, or use an atomic operation such as atomicAdd.

How the exercises model this

The exercises are in Python, so that they run here with no graphics card. One function is already defined for you:

launch(kernel, grid, block, *args)

It calls your kernel once for every thread, in a shuffled order, and passes the thread as the first argument. The names are CUDA's: t.blockIdx.x, t.blockDim.x, t.threadIdx.x, t.gridDim.x. grid and block are pairs, (x, y).

A kernel that is right here is right in CUDA C almost word for word. A kernel that depends on the order the threads run in fails here, as it would on the device.

A complete program in CUDA C

This is the smallest whole program. Type it on a machine with an NVIDIA card, save it as saxpy.cu, and build it with nvcc saxpy.cu -o saxpy.

#include <stdio.h>

__global__ void saxpy(int n, float a, const float *x, float *y) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < n) y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 1 << 20;
    float *x, *y;
    cudaMallocManaged(&x, n * sizeof(float));
    cudaMallocManaged(&y, n * sizeof(float));
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { x[i] = 1.0f; y[i] = 2.0f; }

    saxpy<<<(n + 255) / 256, 256>>>(n, 2.0f, x, y);
    cudaDeviceSynchronize();

    printf("%f\n", y[0]);
    cudaFree(x);
    cudaFree(y);
    return 0;
}

__global__ marks a kernel. cudaMallocManaged asks for memory that both host and device can use, and the system moves it when needed; the older way is cudaMalloc on the device with cudaMemcpy in each direction. cudaDeviceSynchronize waits for the kernel: a launch returns at once, before the work is done. It should print 4.000000.

The same model in Python

Numba compiles a Python function into a real kernel, with the same blocks and threads:

from numba import cuda

@cuda.jit
def saxpy(a, x, y):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    if i < x.size:
        y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]

saxpy[blocks, 256](2.0, x, y)

cuda.grid(1) is the index line, done for you.

What PyTorch does with all this

tensor.to("cuda") is the copy to the device. Every operation on a tensor there is a launch of kernels someone else wrote. Two consequences reach you even if you never write a kernel:

  • Launches return before the work is done. To time something on the GPU, call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock, or you time the launch and not the work.
  • Each launch has a fixed cost. One big batch beats many small ones for that reason, until memory runs out.

What was checked before release: the kernels shown with each exercise, and the complete program above, were compiled as C++ and run on a processor with stand-ins for the CUDA calls. That tests their arithmetic. Nothing was run on a real device, and the Numba lines were not run at all. The Syllabus list under Lists has the programs to write and time on the V100.

lessons.title: MapReduce and message passing
lessons.html:
Threads share one memory. That is convenient and it stops at one machine. To use many machines, each process keeps its own memory, and anything another process needs has to be sent to it.

Message passing

MPI is the standard library for this. You write one program. It is started many times, on one machine or on hundreds, and each copy is told its rank, a number from 0 to size - 1. The copies differ only in what they do with their rank.

#include <mpi.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    int rank, size;
    MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);
    MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &rank);
    MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &size);

    int mine = rank + 1, total = 0;
    MPI_Reduce(&mine, &total, 1, MPI_INT, MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
    if (rank == 0) printf("%d processes, total %d\n", size, total);

    MPI_Finalize();
    return 0;
}

Build it with mpicc sum.c -o sum and run four copies with mpirun -np 4 ./sum. It prints 4 processes, total 10.

The calls come in two kinds:

  • Point to point. MPI_Send and MPI_Recv move data between two ranks. A plain receive waits until the message arrives, so two ranks that both wait to receive before they send will wait for ever. That is a deadlock.
  • Collective. Every rank makes the same call. MPI_Bcast sends one value from a root to all. MPI_Scatter deals an array out in equal pieces and MPI_Gather collects them. MPI_Reduce combines one value from each rank into a single result at the root.

A typical program is: rank 0 reads the input, scatters it, every rank works on its piece, and a reduce or gather brings the answer back. Each rank works out which piece is its own with the block formula from the first lesson.

Inside, a reduce does not have every rank send to rank 0 in turn. The ranks pair up, then the survivors pair up, and so on: about log p rounds instead of p. One exercise has you produce that schedule.

MapReduce

MPI gives full control and expects you to handle everything, including a machine dying halfway through. MapReduce offers much less and handles the rest. You write two functions:

  • map takes one record and returns (key, value) pairs
  • reduce takes one key with all the values that were paired with it, and returns a result

Between them the framework does the shuffle: it gathers all pairs with the same key onto one machine. Counting words is the standard example. Map says ("the", 1) for each word; reduce adds up the ones.

Because a map call depends on nothing but its record, the framework can run it anywhere, and run it again somewhere else if a machine fails. That is the whole trick, and it is why the two functions must not keep any state between calls.

A combiner is a reduce that runs early, on each machine, on the pairs that machine produced, so that ("the", 1) five hundred times travels as ("the", 500) once. It is only safe when combining in pieces gives the same answer as combining all at once. Sums, minimums and maximums are safe. A mean is not: the mean of two means is not the mean of the whole. The cure is to carry a sum and a count, and divide at the very end.

Hadoop is the open implementation: files are cut into large blocks stored on several machines by HDFS, and the map runs on a machine that already holds the block. Spark keeps the same idea, holds the data in memory between steps, and lets you chain many maps and reduces, which suits the repeated passes of machine learning.

The same shape, again

Private partial results, combined at the end:

WherePartial resultCombined by
OpenMPeach thread's private totalthe reduction clause
GPUpairs of elementsrounds of a tree
MPIeach rank's valueMPI_Reduce
MapReduceeach machine's combined pairsthe reducer
Federated learningeach client's update and its sample countthe server's weighted average

The last row is where your research interest sits. Federated averaging is a map on every client and a reduce on the server, and weighting each client by its number of samples is the combiner done properly.
